segments.text: The signal that tells a missile where it is has traveled 20,000 km from a satellite and
by the time it reaches the ground it is weaker than the background hiss of the radio spectrum.
A receiver can only pick it out because it knows exactly what pattern to look for.
A small transmitter, no larger than a lunchbox, that does nothing but send noise on the same
frequency can drown it for many km around.
No bang, no smoke, nothing visibly damaged.
The missile simply stops knowing where it is.
So here is the question.
How can a fight be fought without anyone firing a shot, and why do modern armies spend so
much money on it?
The answer is that almost everything a military does now depends on something that travels
through the air as a radio wave, and a wave can be heard, blocked, or lied to.
Electronic warfare is the contest over that space, and it works in three parts, each of
which exists because the one before it left something open.
Start with the first part, which is simply listening.
Every radar, radio, data link, and navigation device sends out something.
A receiver tuned to the right frequency can catch it, measure it, and say what kind of
emitter it is and in what direction.
A skilled operator can tell one radar from another by the rhythm of its pulses, much as a birdwatcher
knows a call, and can tell one unit from another by their habits.
This is called electronic support, and it is the least visible form of electronic warfare.
It starts long before a war does, with libraries of what everyone's equipment sounds like.
The same listening sits in the cockpit of almost every combat aircraft as a radar warning receiver.
When a hostile radar sweeps over the jet, a tone sounds in the pilot's headset, a symbol
appears on a screen, and a bearing says where it came from.
The pilot may never see the missile that follows.
The first sign of a fight is a sound, and a pilot who has learned what each tone means
has several seconds to react that another would not.
That listening makes the second part possible, which is attack.
If you know the frequency of a radar, you can send noise on the same frequency until the
screen is a snowstorm.
This is jamming in the plane's sense.
A cleverer version is deception.
Instead of noise, the jammer captures the radar's own pulse and sends it back late, so that the
radar sees an aircraft that is a few comolitors farther off than it really is, or a dozen
aircraft where there is one.
A radar tracking a real target may be dragged away from it, so that a missile guided by it
misses by a distance that the crew can measure in hundreds of meters.
There are also cruder tools that work.
Chaff is a cloud of thin metal strips cut to the length of the radar's wavelength, so that
each one returns a strong echo, and a cloud of them hides the aircraft in a blizzard.
Decoys, small powered machines launched from an aircraft, mimic the signature of a larger
one.
In both cases, the idea is the same, which is that the enemy's sensor works, but it has
been given too many things to be sure about.
All of this has a cost, and it is borne by the aircraft, or the unit that does it.
A jammer sends a powerful signal, and a powerful signal is a beacon.
Anyone with a receiver can find it from a long way off, and there are missiles designed
to fly down the beam to the transmitter that is making it.
That produces a strange kind of tension.
The jammer protects, and it also announces, a crew has to decide when to switch it on,
for how long, and from where.
And a good decision is often to keep it off.
So that the aircraft carrying the jammer does not itself get shot down, there are specialized
jets that do nothing else.
A modern standoff jamming aircraft carries pods under its wings and wingtips that are tuned
to the radars of an enemy air defense, and it flies near an attack force to blind the
radars that would see it.
It does not shoot down anything with a gun.
Its work is to make sure that the aircraft behind it are not seen, or are seen too late.
That is why the third part exists, which is protection.
The effort to make your own equipment work in spite of the enemies.
A radio can hop between frequencies hundreds of times a second in a pattern only its partner
knows, so a jammer would have to cover the whole band at once.
A signal can be spread over a wide range of frequencies at such a low power that it sits
below the noise and is invisible to anyone who is not expecting it.
Antennas can be shaped to listen in one direction and ignore the others, so that a jammer to
the side hardly counts.
Each of these tricks is a way of saying that the signal belongs to a conversation, and the
enemy is not part of it.
This is also why electronic warfare has no permanent form.
A technique that works in one month may fail in the next, because the other side has found
the gap and closed it with a software update.
Modern jammers and radars hold a table of known signals that is rewritten as new ones
are heard, and the speed of rewriting is a measure of how good the force is.
A table that takes a year to update is a table of what the enemy used to do.
The most famous example of both sides at work is navigation.
Satellite navigation is so useful that it is built into the guidance of aircraft, missiles,
shells, and drones, and so weak that it is easy to disturb.
In recent wars, jamming has pushed many guided munitions off their targets, and forced designers
to give weapons a second way of knowing where they are.
Some now carry an inertial unit that measures their own movement, a camera that recognizes
the ground beneath them, or both.
The weapon that once depended on one signal now carries a small collection of backups.
Spoofing is the quieter relative of jamming.
Instead of blocking the navigation signal, a spoofer sends a false one that the receiver
trusts, and slowly walks it somewhere else.
A drone whose navigation has been spoofed does not know it is lost.
It continues to fly confidently toward a place that is not where it thinks it is.
There have been reports of ships and aircraft far from any war displaying positions that
were wronged by many kimlotters.
It is much harder to detect than noise, and that is exactly why it is dangerous.
The same ideas work against communications, which is the most vulnerable thing an army
has.
Units that talk on the radio can be found by their transmission, jammed when it matters,
and listened to when they forget.
Modern forces have therefore learned to treat silence as a weapon.
Headquarters move, change frequencies and talk less, and a unit that stays off the air is
hard to find.
An enemy that can hear is an enemy that can target, and the best radio discipline looks, from the
outside, like nothing at all.
The drones from earlier in this series live in this contest every day.
A drone's radio link is a thing that can be found and blocked, so the soldier flying
it often carries a small device that warns of nearby jamming, and the other side carries
one that can see where the drone's operator is standing.
The cheapest weapon on the battlefield and one of the most closely contested portions of the
spectrum are the same thing.
Both sides are fighting for it, and much of that fight is over before anything explodes.
There is a dry irony in all this.
The more a force depends on its networks, the more valuable it becomes to attack them, and
a network that sees everything is also one that can be blinded in one place.
For a century, the way to win a war was to destroy the enemy's army.
Now, a good part of the effort goes toward making the enemy's army deaf, and making sure
that yours is still able to hear.
Which brings us to what is easy to get wrong.
It is tempting to think of electronic warfare as a set of devices, jammers and pods and special
aircraft.
In practice, it is a contest of habits and databases.
The side that has learned more about the other signals in peacetime, and can change its own
faster in war, tends to win.
That is my own reading, but it suggests that the most important piece of equipment in electronic
warfare is a library of recordings and an operator who knows what unusual looks like.
So return to the missile that stops knowing where it is.
Every part, the receiver that listens, the jammer that blocks, the decoy that lies, the radio
that hops, and the backup that looks at the ground, is there because the radio spectrum
is a place everyone has to share and nobody can see.
It has no front line and no terrain.
It is a landscape made of rules, and whoever knows them best moves through it unnoticed.
